exercise1.prompt: Use the datetime module to print the current date and time with a label

cases.name: prints a real date and time
cases.describe: a date and a time in the output

hiddenCases.name: the datetime module is imported
hiddenCases.describe: import datetime, or from datetime import datetime

hiddenCases.name: the time is read when the program runs
the output says what the value is

exercise1.hint: datetime is both a module and a class inside that module, and they are not interchangeable. Look carefully at which one your import gave you a name for.

questions.prompt: Match each standard library module to the job it is for.
right: Dates, times and the differences between them
Reading and writing structured text used by web APIs
questions.explain: The standard library is a set of small, focused modules. Most of learning it is learning which one owns your problem.

questions.prompt: What do you have to install before using the json module?
choices: A JSON parser of your choice
questions.explain: Standard library modules come with Python itself. That is exactly what makes them worth reaching for first.

questions.prompt: You know a module exists but not what its functions expect. Which do you use?
choices: help(module.function), which explains one of them
print(module), which shows the file it came from
type(module), which shows it is a module
questions.explain: dir answers "what is in here" and help answers "how do I use this one". The question asked the second.

questions.prompt:
from datetime ___ datetime

now = datetime.___()
print(now)
questions.explain: The class and the module share a name, which is why this import line looks like it repeats itself. now() is a class method that reads the clock.
